<reason>A close, high-quality debate. PRO set a clear decision test (per public dollar, durable repeated in-person contact among the actually isolated) and kept two live routes alive to the end: the digitally excluded whom apps never reach (never squarely answered by CON), and the evening-hours point that rooms are locked precisely when the lonely are free, which undercut CON's repeated "libraries are open and empty" claim and its "library at 2 p.m." destination. PRO's pressure question on "expecting them where" forced CON into a list of destinations that were either existing rooms or paid spaces, and PRO's closing exploited that cleanly. CON fought well: the symmetry move (rooms are human-mediated too), "loneliness in a crowd," and the sign-vs-road closing analogy were genuinely damaging and forced PRO to concede rooms need programming. But CON's amortization answer only partially repaired the near-zero-marginal-cost claim after conceding humans stand behind every check-in, and CON never engaged PRO's 6–9 p.m. reframing. PRO's two clipped turns were a real execution cost (the homebound point went unanswered and CON rightly pressed it), which keeps the margin thin.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The "expecting them where" exchange: PRO's Q2 forced CON to list destinations that are mostly existing libraries, cafés, congregations, and a 1 a.m. video call; PRO's closing turned this into "an app that succeeds by sending people to a library is an argument for funding the library." CON's sign-vs-road reply was clever but left PRO's point that the evening "road" does not exist largely untouched.</best_rebuttal>
